speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: All of us know of many in our society who desire to do good for others and who care for the less fortunate.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Question is how will the Ministry partner the private and people sectors to create more opportunities for Singaporeans to step forward and, in the process, enable Singaporeans to contribute meaningfully?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Singapore Cares has what I think is a simple but very difficult goal – to make doing good a sticky form of behaviour, to make volunteering and to make thinking about the good of others a habit of mind and a way of life.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But often, we have one-off projects that may have been started by an enthusiastic group whose initial fire has dimmed; such projects are laudable but, if ad hoc, not as powerful as they should be.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need such efforts to be embedded within the structures of our social life.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: What I have in mind is something like Singapore (SG) Cares, which treats people who need help as part of the Singapore family, and sees our commitment in time and effort, supported by different social groups, from families, schools, companies and grassroots organisations.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Can I ask the Minister for an update on SG Cares, what has been done in the past year since its launch, and what his plans are for the future?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In particular, I would like to ask the Minister what data he plans to collect, to measure not just the number of volunteers, but the stickiness of programmes and whether volunteers prefer to stick to one particular type of activity or prefer to try out different things.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Do younger people have less time for volunteering as they begin their careers and families?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If so, what sort of volunteering opportunities are there for them?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I have an idea, especially for people who have never volunteered or who see lack of time as an impediment to doing so: micro-volunteering, where tasks are completed by a volunteer in small increments of time, at his own pace.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They are in short bursts and bite-sized activities, anything from baking a cake for fundraising, graphic design for a charity logo, to knitting beanies for premature babies, or counting plant and animal species for non-profit or research and data gathering, depending on the needs.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: While micro-volunteering may appear to go against the long-term commitment I spoke about earlier, it is, in fact, a useful complement.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Such activities are a good way to start the journey and may lead to a longer-term commitment in the future.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Such volunteers also bolster the core group during peak times.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But I do think all volunteering helps the community and social ties.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is always useful because thinking about the good of others, and not just ourselves, is a vital part of what it means to build a country.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, there are still needs in the community which cannot be fully addressed by machines or paid staff.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need more Singaporeans to step in and step up to help as volunteers who care.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am, therefore, happy that the Government has started the SG Cares movement in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To fully exploit the potential of this meaningful movement, there must be a solid structure, network of services and programmes and a strong human touch.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to organise ourselves effectively so that the total impact is greater than the sum of impact had we acted alone.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Today, we have a myriad of formal and informal groups of volunteer organisations doing community service, serving from their hearts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Still, we also see Singaporeans who would like to serve but are unsure of what they can do, what needs are still unfulfilled and whether the time commitment will be too great for them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, we need to find ways to make serving a priority and organise ourselves better so that busy Singaporeans can just "plug and play" when serving the community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, I would like to ask the Minister for an update on the overall SG Cares movement and how he assesses its impact so far.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What is SG Cares doing to inspire Singaporeans to see community service as a priority in their lives?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Does SG Cares sees itself as, potentially, the national coordinating body for community causes and needs in Singapore, one that consolidates and monitors the list of needs in the communities and resources that are already available, one that identifies the roles and corresponding manpower needed, and one that coordinates and helps everyone clearly see how we can all fit in to help?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In our early days, our forefathers came together, set up community groups, for example, clan associations, to support one another through difficult times.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I remember when I was young, in our neighbourhood, regardless of the kind of housing we had, the whole neighbourhood would look out for one another, everyone chipping in to help one another in times of difficulty or celebrating together.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, last year, in your closing speech for the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) COS, you had said that "SG Cares is not a Government scheme.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is more of giving and volunteering by individuals and groups, and a lot of this is already taking place in our community.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: SG Cares provides an overall umbrella to encourage and support these efforts, to facilitate and drive more outreach".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat, in his Budget Statement this year, had also stressed that it is shared responsibility which is what has made our society what it is today and will keep our community thriving in the years ahead.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It has got to go beyond that to the spirit of giving.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Since then, it has enabled resources to be pooled together and appropriately channelled to those in need.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The acts of kindness publicised on the platform also serve as a source of inspiration to many others.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The movement has immense potential to create a strong and sustainable volunteering ecosystem so that Singapore may be a caring and inclusive home for all.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It is uplifting to note that the Government plans to play a bigger role, through enhanced partnerships with the community to support seniors and those in need.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But the Government has already been working with the grassroots and the voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs).

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The corporations in our country are key players to the field of volunteerism, for they possess ample resources and have the ability to be a significant influencer.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In recent years, more social enterprises are stepping up and they have created many meaningful social projects.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Corporations are different from social enterprises, but they can contribute to the community in a different way.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I think it is important to have a varied approach when it comes to fund-raising and volunteerism.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Sustainability is made a mandatory requirement for all public-listed companies.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Maybe the Government can explore if it can encourage these companies to make volunteerism a good activity for reporting in their annual report to all the stakeholders.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This may help to boost more corporations to engage volunteerism for a good cause.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Technology has the potential to reap huge economic benefits.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Adopting the use of technology to support people in developing a caring and civic culture would be in line with our drive to be a Smart Nation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Thus far, we have platforms like Giving.sg to enable charitable causes to tap on convenience of online tools to gain exposure and collect funds.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There is also SG Cares, which has a website and a mobile app, allowing users to make sense of available projects and causes and so on.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In fact, the SG Cares website as well as mobile app are wonderful tools, and I think the level of awareness, public awareness, is lacking.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, I hope the Government as well as the Ministry can help to push for awareness of SG Cares.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: An article in The Guardian shared statistics that implied a growing use of mobile apps to make donations in the United Kingdom (UK).

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am sure a similar trend is happening in Singapore as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The United Nation's (UN’s) World Food Programme released a mobile app called Share the Meal, and donors can easily make small payments by tapping on their phones.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In an era where contactless payments and one-touch convenience have become a way of life, it is important for charities to keep up with the trends.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Yet, while these apps would help to increase productivity and reduce reliance on manpower, charities, however, chronically fail to embrace them due to the lack of resources to tap on technology in the first place.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It also costs money to hire a professional data analyst or purchase tools to make sense of social media campaigns.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Perhaps SG Cares could think of how to link up mobile apps and software developers with the charities in need.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: With the rising popularity of software developer jobs and careers, SG Cares may even wish to link up with Workforce Skills Qualifications (WSQ) to match inspiring software developers to charities and build up their portfolio and skills.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: At the local level, there are many stakeholders.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The grassroots organisations, the schools, social service organisations and community organisations are all working on a variety of excellent causes on the ground, from participating in environmental issues, helping animals, to befriending and caring for the less fortunate.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In fact, I was looking through the SG Cares website and I was impressed to learn about many previously unheard and unique causes.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am sure there are more out there.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I often hear stories or witness acts of kindness by residents or grassroots leaders that are really taken for granted.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And it saddens me to hear of others criticising or being very cynical of these efforts.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: For example, there is a misconception that students are being forced to participate in activities like Flag Day and that they do so only for the Community Involvement Programme (CIP) points.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It is demoralising, as I know many students and teachers who find meaning in such activities, and it would be terribly unfair for their good work to be misunderstood and tarnished.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: While there should be no expectation of rewards while doing kind deeds, I hope SG Cares will do more to embrace charitable causes from the ground and encouraging more Singaporeans to do so.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I would argue that in every caregiving instance, it is about making a place for the person to age, heal, grow and even to die with dignity.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Designing caregiving approaches need us to think out of the box, to think in a multidisciplinary way.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: St Joseph's Home houses seniors who need various kinds of nursing care and hospice, but it also has a childcare centre there.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In future, the Home will also host programmes for young people.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, youths from the Boys' Home, which is just beside the St Joseph's Home, will come over to the Home on Friday evenings to man the cafeteria and to perform for the residents of the Home.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This design allows for intergeneration care to be practised.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Here, care is relational, not functional; long-term and less temporal.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Such a venture, intergenerational, cross-sectorial and cross-discipline involves multiple stakeholders and multiple Ministries.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In designing it and getting support for such a project, all the stakeholders and Government agencies think out of their comfort zone to facilitate such creative interventions.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In the United States (US), Creative CityMaking Minneapolis is an art-based innovation initiative that pairs city officials with experienced community artists to eliminate disparities.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Creative projects designed by artists, mapping community assets, mapping the needs of the community in housing, transport and healthcare, help the city government to make informed policies.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The artists also design creative projects for city officials to effect cultural change in their work approaches so that they can effectively work with under-represented community.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We can start with the Social Service Office (SSO) by having inhouse artists work with SSO officials and the community to design community projects, mapping out the needs of the community and co-designing good solutions for caregiving issues and other social disparity issues like digital inequality.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In this way, the caring society we aim for is one that comes from collaboration among the people, agencies and policymakers.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is not just the physical and material, but the mental, emotional and spiritual well-being of the people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: The low-income, for instance, often have to work long hours and may not have a strong education background or access to resources.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Therefore, availability is less of an issue, but rather, access.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: How will MSF help to reduce the administrative paperwork and stress that often result from applicants having to approach different organisations for different purposes and having to make sense of the different qualifying criteria?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: The Government has introduced many assistance schemes and programmes and they are calibrated to meet the varying needs of different segments of society, from the elderly to couples with children and those with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: However, the various schemes and programmes across all Government agencies can be difficult to navigate.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Many could find it difficult to understand which scheme or programme best meets their needs or which schemes they qualify for.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, SSO has been doing a good job assisting residents in need.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It gives better accessibility and faster delivery of assistance to many residents.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: How has SSO been collaborating with other Ministries, agencies and the community partners for a concerted effort in tapping resources to assist such families?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Could MSF expand assistance to give permanent solutions to families in need by providing last-mile outreach and care?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I beseech MSF to spare no effort in assisting our less advantaged families, especially those with children.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: These families need the concerted efforts of MSF to get out of their predicaments and have a more level playing field for their children.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I have raised this issue and the provision of holistic care for these less advantaged families in this House repeatedly in the past and I seek your indulgence for repeating it again today.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Could MSF take a holistic approach in helping these families?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Most of the time, these families have a slew of needs, as in housing, income, care for children or care for sick family members and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: They are usually families with low skills, low paying jobs and some are single-income families.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: There is thus an urgency to assist this group of needy Singaporeans with more lasting solutions.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: While they need immediate cash assistance to tide them over, it is more important that they acquire long-term capabilities so that they are able to sustain themselves.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Just giving them ComCare financial assistance will not be able to achieve this aim.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Their needs have to be looked into holistically in order to lift up the family as a whole.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, equipping parents with skills and finding them employment or assisting their spouses to move away from prejudices and mental barriers to employment can be useful.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Their children should be assisted in terms of well-being, health and education.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Most social workers and MSF staff are required to undertake such a hands-on personalised approach to solve the various needs of each family by going the last mile in outreach and care.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: MSF will need to liaise with various Ministries and other relevant agencies and VWOs to give permanent solutions.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Most times, many of their issues cannot be solved overnight.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: So, these families have to be assisted with continuing follow-up.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Only with such last-mile approach can the needy families achieve sustained and long-term benefits.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to adopt this policy urgently to lift this group so that the following generations will not be in the same predicaments as their parents.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In other words, let us give them a better chance of climbing the social ladder.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Extra effort and last-mile approach must be put in to solve their difficulties.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: With better use of information technology (IT), MSF can have faster and better targeted assistance and better follow-up for long-term solutions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is about living healthy and being supported in staying healthy, with homes, families, neighbours, communities all coming together.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The social environment makes a big difference to whether a senior citizen falls ill – whether a sick patient can receive treatment at home, near to home or recover at home without being admitted to hospital.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, community and social support are very important, and this is something that we see even in the developed nations.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Even in Switzerland, with their Swiss standard of living, they have learned this as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, in recent years, in the past few years and going back further decades, hospitals in Switzerland had discovered that, increasingly, patients are being admitted for social reasons because the patients cannot cope at home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It has been published in the literature even as far back as the late 1980s by researchers in Switzerland and these are lessons we can draw from all around the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is also worrying when social deterioration becomes medical deterioration and hospitalisation because a long stay in a hospital bed leads to deconditioning and loss of physical strength.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It makes it harder for an elderly patient to get back on their feet with the same energy as before.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Ultimately, there is no place like home for health or for healing and we should try to find ways to keep health and maintaining health to be focused on the home and the community, with hospital care needed only when deeply necessary.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, there is room for us, as a society, as a community, to learn and improve.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We need to look at social care and health care as different aspects of the same goal when looking after seniors, and all the more so, with an ageing population and smaller families.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The family is still core but we should find ways to involve the community more – young Singaporeans with a spirit for volunteering, or seniors who are energetic and want to reach out to their peers and in friendship and fellowship.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can the Minister tell us how we can strengthen community support for seniors, in a sustainable way?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Furthermore, social care is also about urban design.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As I spoke about in the Budget Debate last year, urban design can contribute to community engagement or to social isolation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, at the whole-of-Government level, we can look at ways to keep seniors in the community more, and to keep them healthy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, in my maiden speech, I spoke about how we must be: all of us, one Singapore family.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: May our people always grow closer and stronger, at home and in the community, in sickness and health – all of us, one Singapore family.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: This will provide a one-stop centre for a targeted approach in care and also to prevent duplication of effort to achieve the best outcome.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Getting the involvement of grassroots volunteers, VWOs and befrienders will add value to SACs.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: The volunteers from CNS can be channelled as befrienders to assist in the social aspects of the seniors in need and especially those staying alone at home.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Volunteers can also supervise medicine taking, deliver food, escort seniors to hospitals or clean their homes and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: This would be useful for better coverage of our seniors to ensure that no one who needs care is left out.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: I hope AIC can help to have a register of seniors in need and the types of assistance they require so that appropriate assistance can be provided for a better matching of volunteers to provide relevant assistance.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: The SGO can also act as the liaison agency to refer all mobile seniors to join the nearest SAC for physical, mental and social well-being.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: SGO can also pick up cases that need medical care or follow-up to AIC.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: The objective is to encourage Singaporeans to be caring towards others, especially towards the less well-off in our society.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: It is also to encourage Singaporeans to have a volunteering culture where people readily give assistance to the vulnerable, needy, seniors and the less advantaged families.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: It will be good if we can also promote graciousness in the society where Singaporeans are considerate and caring to families, friends and neighbours in our everyday life.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: This register will help them better by providing a convenient one-stop matching service of available volunteers to the recipients by enabling appropriate needs to be dispensed and without duplication of services.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: I believe MSF is the right Ministry to collate all those in need as MSF receives many requests for assistance from residents.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: MSF may need to do a last-mile approach here with staff putting in more efforts to rigorously find out the relevant needs of those in difficulty.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Such a detailed register will enable urgent cases to be detected and attended to more promptly.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Good capture of information and data can help those in need efficiently and in a targeted way to achieve better outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Mr Chairman, with your permission, may I display some slides on the screens?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This lies at the heart of the SG Cares movement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Singaporeans have always believed in helping one another.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We believe in caring for the vulnerable and less fortunate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We believe in supporting our seniors in their golden years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And we believe in standing together as a nation through good times and bad.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This spirit of caring has carried us through many moments of crisis, whether it was the Hotel New World collapse in 1986, the severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) outbreak in 2003 or the severe haze in 2013.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As we go about our daily lives, we benefit from extraordinary acts of kindness, some spontaneous and some organised by those who care.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: One such incredible effort which we recently saw was the project called Wheels@Ubin, an initiative by Dennis Quek and Wilson Ang, two Singaporeans who care.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They believe that no part of Singapore should be inaccessible to any Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They wanted to let wheelchair users and persons with disabilities experience the rustic charm and beauty of our offshore islands, notably Pulau Ubin.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: What was impressive and heart-warming was how businesses, public agencies and departments, volunteers, VWOs, community organisations and educational institutes came together to make this possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, Singapore Mass Rapid Transit (SMRT) taxi drivers with mobile ramps fetched participants on wheelchairs as well as caregivers from their homes, wherever it was in Singapore, to Changi.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, at the Changi Sailing Club, as the fleets of taxis came one after another, volunteers welcomed the participants and fitted them with life jackets.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They were then brought on board a Republic of Singapore Navy fast craft by the Republic of Singapore Navy (RSN) officers, men and women.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Third, upon arriving at Ubin, the visitors were welcomed by colleagues from the National Parks Board (NParks) and entertained throughout their visit by volunteers from the Republic Polytechnic and Ngee Ann Polytechnic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Fourth, volunteer doctors and nurses took personal leave to set up a medical facility to provide backup medical support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They came from various healthcare institutions and formed one medical team.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Wheels@Ubin shows us that our commitment to inclusivity and universal access can go beyond words to become deeds that make our visions reality.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Wheels@Ubin is a good example, but just one of many, many examples of how we can create opportunities to enable and empower people to contribute and give, so that giving becomes a social norm and, as Ms Jessica Tan says, a way of life, an important cornerstone of our social compact, celebrated every day in ways both big and small.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It can change mindsets, cultivate empathy, dismantle prejudices and bring people from all walks of life together for a common cause.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will put us in a better position to confront our challenges together, such as rapid cycles of economic disruption, growing social needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: At the same time, it will let us tap into the opportunities that come with having more Singaporeans live longer, healthier and active lives, growing social entrepreneurship and innovative technologies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Through Singapore Cares, we can become an even more caring and inclusive society, not because we say or wish it to be so, but because each and every one of us is a living testament to this: a nation of givers – not by word, but by action and by deed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Singapore Cares is a movement to identify and share about needs on the ground, shape volunteering opportunities and match givers to causes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have also coordinated local networks of assistance, encouraged corporate and individual giving, and inspired ground-up efforts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are greatly encouraged by many who have stepped forward and answered the call to make Singapore a more caring and inclusive home.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: One organisation which has responded to this call is Pantropic, a data protection company, which actively promotes volunteerism amongst its employees.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Since July last year, staff from Pantropic have been volunteering with Lion Befrienders, a VWO which provides friendship and care for seniors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The company has allowed employees to schedule their time flexibly so that they can take time off during office hours and during the work week to accompany seniors for their medical appointments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And they do so about twice a month on average.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This relieves the staff from Lion Befrienders, allowing them more time to attend to others in need.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The seniors benefit from an expanded circle of friendship with these volunteers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And it is commendable that Pantropic has come forward to contribute actively in this way, despite being a small company with only about 12 employees.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As SG Cares takes root, I am confident that we will see more such successful partnerships.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Even as we celebrated diverse expressions of caring at the inaugural SG Cares carnival in January this year, we looked towards doing more.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, we can better mobilise those who want to help.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Many individuals and organisations wish to volunteer but may not know about the causes and areas of need.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We can think of more ways to reach out to prospective volunteers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, we can better coordinate the help rendered.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: An individual may be receiving help from multiple agencies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Organisations on the ground may focus on specific services and may not be conscious in seeking and working with partners to provide more holistic and thorough support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Third, the way we help can be more sustainable and scalable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will require us to increase the capacity and capability of VWOs and givers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Government, corporate partners and the community can also better direct our energies in an informed, coordinated and sustainable way, supported by good platforms and working arrangements.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our three Ministries have come together today to underscore and support the efforts of SG Cares, which is a people movement, and set out our contribution to this movement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ministers Gan Kim Yong and Grace Fu will speak more about their Ministries' efforts immediately after I speak.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Chairman, for my part, let me share how MSF sees SG Cares as integral to our work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The social service sector has its roots in the spirit of caring and the efforts of those who cared since our early days.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Many VWOs in Singapore have long and distinguished histories, bearing testament to the deep roots of philanthropy and volunteerism in our nation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As mentioned by Ms Jessica Tan, our forefathers banded together to help one another and formed community and self-help groups, such as clan associations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Those who did well in Singapore, such as Tan Tock Seng, Hajjah Fatimah and P Govindasamy Pillai, paid it forward and set up institutions to meet the needs of their fellow men and women.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our VWOs will continue to play a critical role in serving beneficiaries, and in rallying and inspiring the community to care for those who need help.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To meet the demands of the future, we must support them in their drive to be even more effective and innovative.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will continue to build up our social service sector, by strengthening capabilities and ensuring that we continue to attract capable professionals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: At the same time, we will draw on the spirit passed down from the Pioneers and encourage the community to partner the efforts of the Government and the sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I will speak in more detail about MSF's efforts for the social service sector later.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our clients today can face and do face very complex issues and challenges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Individuals and families may have multifaceted needs that require support from multiple agencies, VWOs and community groups, over a sustained period of time, before they can stand on their own feet again.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is, therefore, important, as Mr Amrin Amin has mentioned, to have a concerted and coordinated effort to tackle our social challenges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: By better mapping our needs and tightening coordination and integration of services, we can maximise the impact of social services and public resources entrusted to us.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: At the same time, we can better harness and channel community resources to complement efforts by the Government.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our SSOs will be key to transforming social service delivery.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will better coordinate service delivery and improve client support through the SSOs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, we will equip frontline officers in Government agencies and community organisations with the knowledge to provide clients with basic information and referrals to schemes and services to address their needs, beyond those offered by the agency they first approached.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will start with the SSOs, HDB and People's Association (PA) offices at our local community clubs, which are common touchpoints for residents in need.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Eventually, we will extend this to other touchpoints, including medical social workers and school counsellors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have also established referral protocols to link up partners to support our clients.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For instance, we have been rolling out an SSO-Family Service Centres (FSCs)-Schools referral protocol so that schools know when and how to refer students and their families to the SSOs and FSCs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will complete the rollout to all General Education schools by the end of this year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, we will make it more convenient for clients to apply for assistance schemes and services from different agencies by sharing information and assessments across agencies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As far as possible, they should not need to submit the same documents, repeat their circumstances, or fill in multiple application forms asking for similar information.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will help reduce the burden often faced by low-income individuals and households seeking help, who may already be in distress or urgent need.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, if a client living in public rental housing is receiving ComCare assistance from SSO and we observe that he is unable to keep up with rent, the SSO will share its assessment with HDB to consider a reduction in rent.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will progressively extend this to the mainstream schools, polytechnics and Autonomous Universities (AUs).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will allow them to focus on obtaining or sustaining their employment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These clients will also be assessed for additional financial support, without having to make separate applications.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will continue to explore more ways to reduce the burden on individuals and households in need.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: At the same time, we are mindful not to do this indiscriminately, so that we do not inadvertently erode people’s will to be self-reliant, or create, for that matter, a large cliff effect where multiple lines of assistance come up for review at the same time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Third, we will strengthen cross-agency coordination so that clients receive more holistic and coordinated assistance from the agencies and VWOs that are supporting them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In complex cases where multiple agencies and VWOs are involved, the case lead may not be obvious.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: SSOs will assign a case lead, depending on the client’s underlying issues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The case lead should step up to coordinate among agencies and VWOs, to work on a common plan of action for the client.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Where necessary, cases will also be escalated to the parent Ministry or agency for flexibility to be exercised.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Already, five SSOs are co-located with or near Workforce Singapore (WSG) or Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) career centres, or provide job matching and skills upgrading services for low-income residents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Two months ago, SGO officers serving Taman Jurong and Jurong Spring started operating at the SSO at Taman Jurong.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Similarly, the SGO serving the Marine Parade area will be co-located with the SSO at Geylang Serai from the second half of this year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will support closer collaboration between the SSO officer and SGO officers in supporting clients, especially elderly clients, and planning for programmes and services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Where co-location is not practical, we are looking into video-conferencing for clients to communicate with officers from other agencies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Clients at the SSO who need to have discussions with case officers from SG Enable, SNTC or HDB when applying for services will be able to do so from the SSO, rather than having to separately visit SG Enable at Lengkok Bahru, SNTC in Tiong Bahru or the HDB branch office, wherever that may be.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The initiatives I have spoken about will make the SSO of the future more of a single touchpoint for residents with financial and other social needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A family of four living in a public rental flat applies for ComCare assistance at the SSO.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They have one child with special needs and another studying in ITE.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In addition to the assistance provided by the SSO, the family will be able to access schemes and services from SG Enable for their child with special needs, without having to travel to their offices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If their ComCare assistance is approved, the child studying in ITE will be considered by ITE to receive a bursary, without having to separately apply for one.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And if the family needs to have discussions with the HDB branch office about their rental situation or whether they are eligible for the Fresh Start Housing Grant, they can do so via video-conferencing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And we will tap on the network of the grassroots and the local community to better assist these families as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As social needs evolve, we will continue to work to make sure that our SSOs are equipped to handle the evolving, complex and varied needs of those we assist, to help them get back on their feet again.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The SSOs are also in a good position to foster collaboration and partnerships within the local community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Currently, SSOs have good working relationships with different Government agencies and community partners.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Going forward, the SSOs will step up efforts to bring together community partners to forge a picture, a better picture of local needs, gaps and resources.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: With this common understanding, community organisations will be better able to develop local schemes and programmes, and mobilise and organise volunteers under SG Cares.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In doing so, community and Government efforts will complement each other to contribute towards better social service outcomes and a caring nation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Chairman, I have spoken about the spirit of caring that animates SG Cares and how this same spirit drives the social service sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: None of us got to where we are purely on our own.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Chairman, may I also have your permission to display some slides?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will continue to plan ahead for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Since 2011, we have expanded our healthcare capacity to help seniors age in place.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are continuing to develop new models of care and improve the affordability of eldercare services.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are also enhancing our Seniors’ Mobility and Enabling Fund (SMF) and expanding the Community Silver Trust (CST) fund to cover active ageing initiatives.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Preparing for our ageing population is a whole-of-nation, whole-of-Government endeavour, which is why we launched the Action Plan for Successful Ageing in 2015 to drive collective action in areas, such as employability, senior volunteerism, health and wellness, housing and transport.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Dr Amy Khor gave an update of the action plan in Parliament last month.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I agree with Dr Tan Wu Meng that we must address the needs of seniors holistically.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Seniors often have multiple needs, and we can better coordinate services among partners and stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is why we piloted the Community Networks for Seniors (CNS) in 2016 to mobilise and coordinate efforts of community volunteers, service providers and other stakeholders in each community to care for seniors.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In Tampines, for example, the Evergreen SAC and the Residents' Committees (RCs) work together to organise regular active ageing activities to keep seniors well and active.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We recently started a Community Nurse Post at Evergreen SAC, where a nurse from Changi General Hospital (CGH) is available once a week to help conduct health checks and follow-ups for residents.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For lonely seniors, volunteers and block representatives visit and befriend them.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Care Line, a 24/7 telecare and befriending service, is also available.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Should seniors require a home visit to check in on them, the Singapore Red Cross volunteers can be activated.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are making two structural moves to achieve this.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: First, the repositioning of PGO as SGO, housed within the AIC, will help extend our outreach efforts to seniors beyond the Pioneers and tap on the capabilities and services of AIC.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Some 3,000 volunteers have been trained as Pioneer Generation (PG) Ambassadors since 2014.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: They have done good work and many of them have established personal relationships with the seniors they care for.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In fact, one in four PG Ambassadors are themselves seniors aged 60 and above.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The conversion of PGO to SGO reflects the Government’s commitment to proactively reach out to our seniors, to engage them, understand their needs and care for them.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I agree with Dr Lily Neo, who suggested that the new SGO act as a liaison agency for seniors to proactively connect them to services in the community.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As mentioned earlier by Minister Desmond Lee, my Ministry will also be working with the SSO to do this.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Moving forward, SGO will do more targeted outreach to bring preventive health and wellness programmes to seniors.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For those with multiple needs, they can be quickly connected with relevant health and social support services under AIC.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: One example of a senior who has benefited from CNS is Mdm Lim.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: She is now in her 70s and used to be a lively Chinese opera singer but spent more time alone at home after retirement.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Thanks to a PG Ambassador, Madam Lim is connected to TOUCH Community Services, which subsequently helped her install grab bars in her home, arranged for medical escort and transport services for her medical appointments and also linked her up with Meals on Wheels so that she gets proper meals.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Today, she attends the National Trades Union Congress' (NTUC’s) SilverACE Senior Activity Centre at Taman Jurong regularly and even takes up taichi at the nearby Community Centre (CC).

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I am cheered to know many helping hands are working together to care for her through CNS.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The transfer of MSF’s social care functions to MOH allows us to deliver support to seniors more seamlessly, with AIC as our central implementation agency to coordinate all social and health-related services for seniors and their caregivers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This move also allows us to plan ahead for eldercare services at the national level and in a more integrated manner.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As Dr Lily Neo suggested, the transfer of services under the Senior Cluster Network (SCN) from MSF will enable MOH to better integrate SCN services into the wider CNS.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For example, MOH can now engage service providers to discuss new opportunities for SACs to help seniors age in place, such as through active ageing programmes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The progress we make in strengthening intergenerational bonds will shape our social fabric in the future.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We see this happening in many purposeful ways.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For example, St Joseph’s Home, which Mr Kok Heng Leun mentioned earlier, has a childcare centre and intergenerational playground co-located with the nursing home, creating many opportunities for shared experiences like meals and activities.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At Bedok Orchid RC, students from Temasek Junior College read newspapers and share current affairs with seniors every week, including the Budget.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Not only do both parties gain new insights, they also form new friendships.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Volunteerism is another way through which we unlock our community resources.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We can also harness the immense wealth of knowledge and experience of older volunteers who continue to contribute to the society, as Dr Tan Wu Meng and Dr Lily Neo suggested.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: A good example is Mr Eric Teo, whom I met last month.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Eric is 78 years old and has been volunteering actively at Siglap for the past five years.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In particular, he helps out with the Health Peers Programme run by CGH and the South East Community Development Council (SECDC).

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Eric keeps himself busy by encouraging fellow seniors in Siglap to go for health screenings and he visits the residents to raise awareness of diabetes prevention and management.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In the process, his volunteer work helps keep him fit!

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Mr Eric Teo exemplifies the spirit of SG Cares and shows us how seniors, too, can care for fellow seniors.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I hope his experience inspires more Singaporeans, regardless of age, to come forward to volunteer in the community, so that we make SG Cares an enduring movement.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Minister Grace Fu will speak more on volunteerism in her speech.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Last but not least, several Members touched on the role of caregivers in the Budget Debate.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We recognise the dedication of caregivers and the important role they play in caring for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: My Ministry will provide greater support for caregivers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have also rolled out financial schemes to help defray the costs of care and caregiver training.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Going forward, there is room to do more.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Emotional and timely support is important for caregivers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are working on new approaches, to embed dedicated support for caregivers within eldercare centres.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For example, support could take the form of phone conversations with caregivers, face-to-face meetings or even home visits.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have a national toll-free hotline for seniors and their caregivers, the Singapore Silver Line (1800-650-6060), for assistance regarding our community care services and schemes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: MOH and AIC will continue to take on board feedback from caregivers and work closely with our partners to support them.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Mr Chairman, let me say a few words in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: (In Mandarin):   Mencius once said, "Love the elderly as you would love your own aged parents".

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We must respect and care for our seniors who are an integral part of our society.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Government will do our best to help our seniors in their golden years.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: However, this cannot be done without the help of families and the community at large.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We must work together to build a caring society for all ages.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This way, seniors can age gracefully and confidently among their family, friends and community.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: (In English): Mr Chairman, I look forward to working with fellow Singaporeans to foster a caring society in the spirit of SG Cares.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Chairman, with your permission, I will display some slides.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Many Singaporeans agree that Singapore is a caring and cohesive society but there is still much more that we can do to be a caring people.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: MCCY will work with community and corporate partners, along with MSF and MOH, to support SG Cares.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In line with Dr Lily Neo's suggestion, we want to foster a culture of consideration and contribution, where every citizen is ready to step forward, engage in service to others, and contribute to build a better home for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: When Singapore was finding its feet as a young nation, they made sacrifices to build a better future for all.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: They exemplified the kampung spirit so vital to nation-building.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Today, many are still doing their part to help fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Recognising that seniors tend to stay at home most of the time, Mdm Jumiah started giving qigong lessons in 2013 to promote healthy living in her neighbourhood.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: She takes what she has learnt from her qigong master and teaches a group of up to 50 residents in easy-to-follow qigong exercises.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: With her nursing experience, she also shares tips for healthy living with them.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This is so useful for the elderly as it is right in their neighbourhood, and it is an ideal way for seniors to keep active in their retirement age.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We want this giving spirit to be passed on to each succeeding generation.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To support MSF's efforts to enhance social service delivery on the ground through its SSOs and MOH's expansion of CNS and repositioned SGO, we now need more volunteers than ever to address our growing social and healthcare needs.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As Ms Tin Pei Ling shared, there are many passionate Singaporeans volunteering, whether through formal or informal ways.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Yet, there are also many others who are willing but do not know where, who or how to help.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Some may not know what the available volunteering opportunities are or where the needs are in their local community.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Some may only have little time to give because of work and family commitments.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Others could be too shy to approach neighbours who seem to need help.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: These are some of the barriers that stop us from reaching out to help and do our part.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Through SG Cares, we hope to break down these barriers.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We want to create a society where everyone both gives and receives the care and support they need.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We want Singaporeans to enjoy a culture of neighbourliness and rekindle the 'kampung spirit' within our communities.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: My colleagues and I believe this is possible if we all do our part to help our neighbours, nurture our youths and serve our seniors, so that no one is left behind.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As part of the SG Cares movement, my Ministry will work through corporates and the community while leveraging technology to make it easier and more meaningful for a person to volunteer.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will focus our efforts on encouraging corporate Singapore to step forward and do its part.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As Dr Lim Wee Kiak pointed out, corporates must be key players in the field of volunteerism.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Many of us spend significant hours at work and want to work with a company that does good for society.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Corporates have the ability to organise and mobilise their employees for social good through Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiatives.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Once we leave school and enter the workforce, we volunteer a lot less often because there are other competing priorities.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But through organised CSR activities that are scheduled around our work commitments, we can continue to do our part.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: One example is the partnership between the Post Office Savings Bank (POSB) and NTUC Health.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: NTUC Health is a social enterprise that provides health and eldercare services.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: POSB, as we know, is a bank with a network of branches.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: By adopting flexible volunteer hours and matching employees to an NTUC Health nursing home close to the POSB branches they work at, this partnership saw POSB employees conducting bi-weekly activities, such as morning exercise therapy and breakfast with residents, at NTUC Health nursing homes.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This has brought joy to the residents and helped POSB employees grow a sense of pride in their company and a sense of compassion for our frail elderly.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will continue to help companies in their CSR journey, through the Company of Good, a programme by the National Volunteer and Philanthropy Centre (NVPC) to help companies give more strategically, sustainably and meaningfully.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As part of this programme, we will grow corporate leaders for giving under the Company of Good Fellowship.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will also work through the Community Development Councils (CDCs).

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: With a good understanding of the needs on the ground as well as their network of community partners, the CDCs can help to connect corporates to local CSR opportunities.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling also reminded us of the need to organise volunteer opportunities better so that busy Singaporeans can just "plug and play", making it convenient to do good.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are studying the landscape and will work with partners to explore new ways to organise tasks that will enable neighbours to help one another and take care of their neighbourhood.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This will enable more Singaporeans to be involved and feel a greater sense of ownership for the community they live in.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Additionally, the National Council of Social Service (NCSS) has been working with SSOs to restructure roles, ensuring that they are both suitable for volunteers and meet the needs of the community.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: NCSS is also helping SSOs build up capabilities to manage their volunteers well and deploy them meaningfully so that they feel that they are not "just another volunteer" but someone who is making a difference to the community.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak asked about the use of technology to support people in nurturing a caring civic culture.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Technology has made it easy and convenient for us to provide quick help, collaborate and form community.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will study how to harness the power of technology for social good and provide a one-stop avenue that Dr Lily Neo spoke about, where Singaporeans, especially those with the desire to help but do not know where or how to start, can easily find volunteering opportunities.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The recently launched SG Cares app is a good start.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It is a free mobile app that enables everyone to be plugged into the community of volunteers and opportunities.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will continue to enhance the application to provide a good user experience and build a social network where volunteers can share experiences, learn from one another and serve the community together.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: With technology, we can reach out to show we care, at the touch of our fingertips.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak spoke about the good work that many are doing on the ground.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are fortunate to have many helping hands in the community.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But, as Minister Heng Swee Keat aptly puts it, "our many helping hands need to work hand-in-hand." Under SG Cares, one role for the Government is to facilitate better coordination among the various helping hands NVPC, NCSS, social and healthcare organisations, corporates and the community so that we can mobilise volunteers to meet needs on the ground.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In Jurong East, various stakeholders work together to serve the seniors in different ways.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: They are supported by a network of SSOs with a central coordinator, in this case, Loving Heart Multi Service Centre.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It receives referrals from grassroots networks and the SSO on seniors who require support, links up with partner organisations, refers residents to service providers, and mobilises community organisations and support.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Loving Heart also engages volunteers from partner schools nearby to help in the Centre's activities.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The SG Cares movement has helped to bring these stakeholders together to map out the needs, roles, resources and areas where we need more volunteers.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: By combining our efforts and resources, we have a better picture of the needs in each community and how the various partners can work together to provide more seamless and citizen-centric support.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Say, for example, a senior who has difficulty walking and living on his own is discharged from the hospital.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Understanding that the senior will require home medical and nursing care, a Medical Social Worker at the hospital refers him to the AIC, which gets him connected with the CNS.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: A CNS coordinator will link up with the SSO and various SSOs in his neighbourhood to provide coordinated assistance and support services to the senior.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: However, the CNS, SSO and other SSOs cannot address all his needs on their own.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This is where we, as neighbours and volunteers, can step up and play our part.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: You do not need money, special skills or a lot of time.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If you are an outgoing individual with time to spare, you can volunteer as a befriender to visit him monthly and check out how he is doing.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If you cannot volunteer regularly, you can still help with ad hoc tasks, such as buying groceries or changing a light bulb.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: You can be alerted to these tasks through a tasking app if you live or work nearby.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If you are volunteering as part of your company's CSR, you can be on the "Meals-on-Wheels" roster and help deliver meals to him.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Or if you happen to be his neighbour, you can just drop by his home once in a while, to say "Hi" and to see if he needs any help.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Just as importantly, we seek to enable fellow Singaporeans to step forward as caring citizens and good neighbours to bridge that last mile of care that only family, friends and community can provide.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: At the end of the day, SG Cares is about the kind of society we wish to live in.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We believe that a strong society is one that leaves no one behind and one that focuses on helping the vulnerable amongst us.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: A strong society is one where the civic spirit is strong and where citizens contribute to causes they believe in.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I am not sure whether this is a first time, but certainly it is significant for us to note that we have three Ministers from different Ministries coming together to speak on one topic under one Head.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: The processes to ensure and encourage empathy, however, are very complex and perhaps not always possible to put in place.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Our approach to designing social policies and programmes reflect the values of our society.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: The "Many Helping Hands" approach is the foundation of our social policy.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Ultimately, it is the shared values of Singaporeans that are at the heart of our social compact.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: It helps us weather difficult times together, to move us together and forward to success.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: In recent years, we have been focused on making sure low-income households have a roof over their heads, that every child has access to food, shelter and education.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: But in today's Singapore, all this may not be enough to get them up the social mobility ladder.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: As we continue to face widening income inequality, the Government's approach to these challenges will continue to be based on the principles of "family" as the first line of support.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Even if this is so, if "family", defined in the widest possible way, is the first line of support, sometimes, family members just have no means or resources.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: I have heard of an organisation that gives out book prizes to primary school students who show an aptitude in Maths and Science, to further expose them to opportunities outside of school to fan their passion for sciences.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: They are supposed to embark on a science project of their interest over the school holidays with an assigned mentor/volunteer and put up a show-and-tell.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: However, before the journey commences, some of them drop out; they have no one to transport them to and from the discussion venue as their parents are working on weekends.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: The intention to help exists but implementation can be better.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: That they win medals is due to their hard work, talent and their families, but also, dare I say it, luck that some of them are rich.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: No one who braves a daily 90-minute commute on the public transport will not be hard-pressed to perform at the same level.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: We need to guard against inequality in Singapore; some are more tolerable than others.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: It is up to us to stand against those forms and those extents of inequality that will impact Singaporeans’ ability to live dignified and meaningful lives.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: The Prime Minister has explained that there is a concerted and coordinated effort among Government Ministries to tackle these challenges together in various fora.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Specific to the social service sector, what is MSF's contribution towards tackling these critical issues?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: And how does it intend to work with other Ministries to ensure that all facets to tackling inequality are addressed?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: How do MSF's programmes encourage and reflect the values of self-reliance, empathy and compassion?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With regard to the social service sector, MSF has taken a holistic approach in its efforts to improve social mobility by providing upstream support and strengthening the sector.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: And this we can see in the help that is given to beneficiaries through SSO, and also through what the Minister is sharing in terms of the plans to enhance and strengthen SSO.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: To enable every child to have the right start, access and the quality of preschool education are important.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Preschool and early childhood development platforms are not just about providing childcare but also the environment for our children to develop and build confidence for social integration and life.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: In fact, this is the case for all throughout our learning journey and, especially now, with continuous learning.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With the technological shifts and disruptions that are confronting us, digital capabilities and skills will be crucial for individuals to thrive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Because with these skills, it will help translate ideas and talent for impact.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With these trends, the early childhood sector will need to look at how to better support young families and children for the digital world, specifically those in the lower-income families.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Parliament recently discussed mitigating income inequality, ensuring social mobility and enhancing social integration.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: The Prime Minister had explained that there is a concerted and coordinated effort among Government Ministries and agencies to tackle these challenges together in various fora.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Specific to the social service sector, how is MSF tackling these critical issues?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Is the number for homelessness getting bigger over the years?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Does MSF monitor the reasons for those who sleep on the streets?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Is there any ongoing outreach to them island-wide in order to understand their problems?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Could MSF follow up individually and provide long-term solutions?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Many of them may have a variety of problems, such as family feuds, HDB housing issues, mental issues, employment and financial issues.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: These issues will need close follow-up with various Ministries and assistance rendered to achieve permanent solutions.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Unless we provide such assistance, it is going to be an unending problem.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: It is futile trying to discourage them sleeping on the streets by chasing them away as they will just go sleep at another location.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: I have had residents sleeping in Chinatown staircases or plastic chairs due to frequent quarrelling with co-tenants in HDB rental flats due to incompatibility of personality and character.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Our housing policy requires two individuals to share HDB rental homes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: This can create a lot of problems, especially for those having to stay with strangers because they do not have family members to rent with.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: This is especially so for many seniors who have difficulty adjusting due to their seniority.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: There are some individuals who just cannot live with strangers despite many transfers of HDB rental homes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Apart from sleeping on the streets, MSF may also encounter them coming for ComCare as they cannot continue working, because they cannot sleep at night or they face daily living issues due to unreasonable co-lessees, according to them.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Could MSF intervene in such cases and recommend for these individuals to rent HDB flats on their own, following psychological assessments?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Many homeless people do not like the shelter homes, such as Pelangi Shelter, as they prefer to have freedom to move about.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Can MSF provide a better concept for shelter homes catering to the homeless group, giving them the flexibility of going out and about, staying in touch with their friends in the community and continuing to work whilst residing in a shelter home?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, Sir, Singapore has acceded to the Convention of the Rights of the Child, which defines children as persons below the age of 18.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Being a signatory, Singapore is obliged to take all measures for the implementation of the rights recognised in the Convention.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If not, what are some issues the Government is grappling with?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: By and large, it would be a natural instinct on the part of the parents to discharge this duty.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Unfortunately, from time to time, there have been cases of parents abdicating their responsibility towards their children.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Just on 2 March 2018, during the COS debate on the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), we heard the hon Minister for Home Affairs providing some examples of serious child abuse and neglect.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I recently had occasion to deal with a case which threw into focus the current requirements under the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Sometime in the second half of last year, I met the parents of a 7-year-old boy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The boy’s father sought my help to deal with a problem he had with a Police Officer.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The mother was a young lady who was rather quiet.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Whilst I was talking to the father, I noted that the boy sported long hair; it was even below his shoulders!

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Curious as to how he could keep such long hair in school, I asked the boy which school he was studying in.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To my surprise, I learnt that he was not registered in primary school.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a violation of the Compulsory Education Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a matter of fact, the boy did not go to kindergarten as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Both parents were content for their son to be at home and schooled by his mother.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, prior approval from the Director-General of Education, as required under the Compulsory Education Act, was not sought.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I must add that, from a physical perspective, the boy appears to be reasonably taken care of.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My community leaders engaged the father and attempted to persuade him to register his son for school as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Based on the last update I received, despite six months of trying, the boy has yet to be registered.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He is eight years old now this year.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Officers from MOE and MSF have been engaging the father and trying to persuade him to send his son to school.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under the Act, as the boy is physically well taken care of, it would not be possible to intervene under the Act on the ground that the parent neglected to ensure that he is enrolled in a primary school.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In response to a Parliamentary Question (PQ) I filed in November 2017 suggesting that the criteria under the Act be expanded to include situations whereby a parent neglects sending a child to primary school, the Hon Minister replied that the reasons for a child not attending school are often complex.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister opined that it was not necessary to extend the criteria under the Act on the basis that the framework provided under the Compulsory Education Act already covers this aspect.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I respectfully seek a reconsideration of the Government's position for the following reasons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, I think we can all agree that it is critical for a child to attend primary school for the sake of his own development and to create the common experience necessary for the child to identify himself as part of our community and nation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is the raison d'etre behind the enactment of the Compulsory Education Act in the first place.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
