text: In addition, our future social needs are growing in complexity and intensity and will inevitably demand more from the sector and our professionals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is, therefore, timely to reflect on how the sector can be better prepared for future demands and challenges to sustain and also to multiply their impact.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is a strategy developed for the social service sector by members of the Social Service Sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The first is empowered individuals, families and communities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The social service sector believes in treating everyone, especially the vulnerable, with dignity and care.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The way help is given to individuals and families should empower them, enable them to take personal responsibility for their lives and build resilience.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The second is effective VWOs that deliver quality, innovative and sustainable solutions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: VWOs deliver more effective and impactful services when they are well-run, healthy and innovative.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Good organisations can create more impact with the same amount of resources.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The third is a caring, collaborative and impactful social service ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The social sector does not exist in isolation, but seeks to work with the wider community, bringing everyone together to contribute our skills, time and resources to care for the vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The impact is not only on those being helped, but also in transforming the nature and character of society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, I am very glad that VWO sector partners and NCSS have come up with this shared vision.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Many VWOs have already rallied behind that vision and exemplify it in their work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I hope this remains a good guidepost to shape the work of the sector towards stronger collective impact.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our social workers, therapists, psychologists and teachers all work to improve and shape the lives of their beneficiaries, with many of them going the extra mile.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: One such dedicated professional is Ms Teo Yafen, a speech and language therapist at the Cerebral Palsy Alliance of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: She helps adults with disabilities overcome speech impediments, so that they can better integrate and contribute to society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: She has been actively advocating the importance of speech therapy for her clients, as she believes it improves their health, safety and ability to communicate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, speech therapy services ensure that any early signs of swallowing difficulties in persons with cerebral palsy are recognised and managed, preventing complications, such as chest infections.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ultimately, Yafen believes in a Singapore where persons with disabilities are fully integrated and can contribute to the community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Many of those who work in the social service sector do not do it for the remuneration.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Nonetheless, they deserve to receive a fair and competitive wage and have their contributions duly recognised.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Every three years, MSF reviews the salary norms for Government-funded programmes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, a senior teacher trained in early special needs education may expect an increase of about 8% after the revision.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The updated norms form the basis for NCCS’ Salary Guidelines for the social service sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And I urge VWOs to use these guidelines to guide their wage adjustments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In line with the SkillsFuture movement, we will create more developmental pathways and build up the skills of those who work in the social service sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Under this programme, diploma graduates with less than two years of work experience will undertake studies in Social Work while working as social work associates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Students will take courses from Nanyang Polytechnic’s post-Diploma programme during the first year, followed by a two-year part-time Bachelor's in Social Work programme at SUSS to become qualified social workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: SSG will also provide course fee subsidies and incentives to participants and grants to help participating employers defray the costs of running the programme in their organisations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: WLP is part of a wider effort to open up pathways for individuals to fulfil their professional aspirations and also to support employers in training their employees.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This framework is developed jointly with SSG, our VWOs and social service professionals to help professionals better plan their careers and proactively develop their skills to meet the demands of the sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It will have information on career prospects, skills required for key professions, as well as the learning platforms to develop these skills.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These and other initiatives support VWOs in attracting and grooming good people.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I hope that employees and employers will make full use of them, so that we can become stronger as a sector and fulfil our mission in social service.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Even as we work to build up the social service sector and skillsets of our social service professionals, I am very much aware that the work you do demands a lot of you and from you.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I draw back again to the fundamentals driving the SG Cares movement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: SG Cares is about helping the vulnerable and less fortunate in our society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is equally about a transformation in our national spirit.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When we work to change the lives of others, we also change our own lives for the better.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We become not just individuals concerned with our own interests but part of a larger community of giving, and these activities become a vital and intrinsic part of our identity and social fabric.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We become better people and, collectively, a better society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Government, therefore, should play a role to coordinate, facilitate and make the best use of the community’s efforts and energies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Earlier, Ms Tin Pei Ling asked about volunteerism.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are working to redesign volunteer roles to best match the needs of the organisation and the busy schedules of volunteers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, NCSS partners VWOs to identify their needs before matching them with corporates located ideally in close proximity and encourage them to volunteer regularly to meet these needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are building up the capacity and capability of our VWOs to ensure that volunteers are meaningfully deployed and engaged while volunteering.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are helping our VWOs to develop volunteer management frameworks to enable them to recruit, engage and retain volunteers more effectively to foster sustained volunteering.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are also training and developing the competencies of volunteer managers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In last year’s debate, we spoke about SHARE As One, which is a grant scheme introduced in 2016 to encourage individual and workplace giving and create more volunteering opportunities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Under SHARE, employees donate regularly to the Community Chest through payroll deductions, General Inter-bank Recurring Order (GIRO) or by credit card.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Businesses can use a portion of the Government's matching grant to organise CSR and volunteerism activities, and the rest will be channelled to a fund managed by ComChest to build the volunteer management capabilities of VWOs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: ComChest plays an important role in supporting about 80 VWOs in fundraising so that they can better focus on caring for the disadvantaged.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Programmes supported by SHARE include FSCs and day activity centres for adults with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are also looking to extend this to the private sector, and I hope businesses will enroll for this initiative.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: SHARE as One, as well as ComChest's other efforts, will make giving more sustainable and stable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The sum total of regular and long-term giving by many individuals goes a long way towards helping VWOs and the beneficiaries that they serve.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Chairman, I have chosen to round off my replies by talking about our social service sector because the dedication of those who work in this sector and the sacrifices that they make deserve our respect and support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I am heartened by the generous contributions of donors and the tremendous efforts of volunteers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Because this giving is precious, and because so much heart goes into it, we must make sure that it does not go to waste.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We can and will make our efforts count and maximise our impact on the lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Many of the initiatives I have spoken about today contribute to this drive to build up and better channel resources and services from the Government, community and corporations to those who need it most.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In providing these services and resources, we want to uplift these vulnerable individuals and families and give them the opportunity to take charge, improve their lives and fulfil their aspirations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We wish to build, in the words of our founding Prime Minister, the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew, I quote: a "fair, not welfare, society", where everyone has an equal shot at success.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is the kind of inclusive and caring Singaporean society we aspire to be.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to thank the Ministers for their answers, and I also like to thank the Senior Parliamentary Secretary for addressing the topic of family support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Clearly, I strongly support the idea of having family as the first line of defence.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Still, I would like to ask how MSF balances the need to emphasise family as the first line of defence and the need to help our elderly or the vulnerable in a timely manner.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Second question, in addition to the Families for Life Council, what other organisations seek to promote family life and development?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Are there organisations that cater to the needs of families from various ethnic groups?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Lastly, besides the skills framework and salary guidelines for the social service sector, what other measures are in place to attract and retain good people?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On the elderly, Members would have heard the Minister of Health describe how, under the SG Cares movement, CNS, allows us to tap on the strength of a network of volunteers who live in the community to look out for our seniors and to be able to alert us on occasions of need.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Then, behind the scenes, MOH, MSF and the other agencies will coordinate and try to resolve issues that the seniors face.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The key is to take a practical and not a dogmatic approach to help him.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We recognise that in this day and age, younger people come under a lot of stress with their own work, jobs and families and, therefore, it is a case of them playing their part, but both Government and the community doing more as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On the Member's question about the skills framework and how to attract more people into the social service sector, I have said earlier that remuneration is not something that social service professionals come into the sector to look for.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we certainly need to make sure that it does not fall too far behind median wages in comparable professions elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, we treat our social work professionals and colleagues with dignity and respect.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NCSS works very hard on branding, awareness and outreach to help young people who are thinking of a career to decide whether the social service sector is one area they would like to move into, with not just broad information about the sector but also making available to them information about, say, the disability sector and its challenges and opportunities, young children, the elderly, and so and so forth.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, NCSS, our VWOs and MSF continue to make efforts to reach out through career fairs, branding campaigns, outreach and open houses to continue to bring people into the sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ultimately, it is about people with a heart who want to give back that we want to attract.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Beyond the Families for Life Council, we also have many community agencies that actually play an important role in promoting families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: They include the Centre for Fathering, Fei Yue Community Services, Morning Star Community Services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For example, some of them have their own programmes that we and the laymen would know.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For example, the Centre for Fathering is very well-known for Dads for Life, which, I think, Mr Speaker, is also very actively involved.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Beyond that, we also look at some organisations that look at the ethnic groups and specific groups, for example, the Chinese Development Assistance Council (CDAC), the Council for the Development of the Singapore Malay/Muslim Community (MENDAKI) and the Singapore Indian Development Association (SINDA).

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We are also very happy that, lately, we are seeing more organisations working together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This is something that they believe in, that family development is very important.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: It is not only about helping vulnerable families but also how, as a whole, we can develop and give opportunities for Singaporeans to have good families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I want to share a personal experience, if you allow me, Mr Chairman.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We are all busy and very fortunate to be in MSF where we try to promote family life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I make it a point to spend time with my wife and children since I got married and we are very close together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We help one another, we face challenges together, and it is seldom that I have been home alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: A week ago, I was home alone for about a week plus.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I share quite a number of the activities at home, like washing and cooking.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I do that and I share part of the responsibilities of my wife.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: But one thing I realised when I was home alone was that I missed my family.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I began to feel the "miss" and love for my wife and my children, and I realised that what I did to make my family time was worth it because it came out.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, when my wife and son came back on Monday, then I started to feel a sense of happiness, a sense of fulfilment that what I have done actually brought that happiness and sweetness in my heart and mind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Then I am more determined to spend time, to make time and to say "I still do" to my wife.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, I want to urge Singaporeans to actually make time, spend time with your spouse and be part of the life of your children because it is all worth it and it is something that we all should strive for.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As far as when you are married, you look for happiness together and you want to see how you can journey through your family journey together with your children and your spouse, as part of a bigger family together.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Earlier, the Senior Parliamentary Secretary mentioned that the Early Childhood ITM will be released today.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: For MTL preschool teachers, I would like to enquire whether in this ITM there will be clear career and skills upgrading pathways for MTL teachers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: They, too, look forward to career progression and good pay rises.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: As we all know, the key is about effective case management and coordination.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: In the roadmap, the SSO is in the centre of it all.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: The second point I would like to raise is that I also welcome that the Minister announced that for the lower-income families, in particular, this early upstream approach is key.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: It enables them and gives them a way out.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Is there a way we could almost handhold them to make sure that nothing gets dropped?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Of course, more policies and programmes can and will be rolled out over the course of many years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But implementation is key and coordination on the ground is critical.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is targeted at families and individuals and communities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, the role of the SSOs in this enhanced social service delivery framework is as follows.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: One, to bring networks of communities together at the local level.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I said earlier in my speech that our SSOs will facilitate networking amongst VWOs, FSCs, schools, organisations and grassroots.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Any organisation on the ground that participates either generally or sectorally in supporting the vulnerable and the low income, we want to network with them so that we can work better together.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Individuals may face issues with housing that may pertain to both HDB and CPF.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They may need financial assistance but they would also like to be employed, have the skills needed to get a job so that they can stand on their own two feet.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They may have family members who suffer from health or disability and, as a result, they need caregiving support, disability support or even respite care.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Identifying the whole range of needs around the individuals and not looking at it purely from an agency's point of view will allow us to look at the individual and the family holistically, and see what steps need to be taken together or chronologically in sequence to try to enable them, where possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, that will be what we need for SSOs and our partner agencies to do.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Through networking, we may also be able to unlock community resources that hitherto have not been part of the formal scheme of things.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think that would just allow more people to come in to provide support and to do so holistically in relation to an individual or a family in a way that enables them and not erodes whatever will they have to want to also play their part.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And in a way that does not erode the principle of family as the first line of defence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, support the individual, support the family but, if all else fails, make sure your social safety net is as effective as it can be.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As I said earlier, programmes and policies are there.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That is why KidSTART has put in a tremendous amount of resources.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Because some of the players might be more compliant VWOs but some are really people who just want to do their own stuff.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Because in some of our constituencies, some of us MPs are trying to play that role.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: And sometimes we were successful and sometimes we were not.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: How do we ensure they have the muscle and the support and the resource to do so?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: My second clarification is to do with the Enabling Masterplan.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: A lot of us contributed to it, including members of the public, more than 400, 500 in numbers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: So, I am wondering if there is a more structured and systematic way by which this plan can be updated.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Some may be basic targets, some can be stretched targets.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: And, of course, we know plans are plans, these are five-year plans, things might change.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: How can there be a better, more systematic and structured way to update the ground?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The next clarification is, I brought up three key gaps and I chose the gaps and the examples because I think they are quite genuine and real.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: So, I would like to ask for the Minister and Senior Parliamentary Secretary's update on this.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think the road ahead is not going to be easy − putting in policies, getting agencies to make sure that they provide good service, that they assist people within the schema of that portfolio.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think that is already one task that in Singapore our agencies do well, reasonably well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There is always room to improve but reasonably well, comparatively.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Wanting to coordinate across agencies, making each frontline counter provide information beyond what they already do will be something that we need to push on for many years to come and continuously refresh as officers come and go and join or retire.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, this will be a continuous work-in-progress and will take time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But I firmly believe that many people in the social service sector and also many people in this House whom I have spoken to, believe that if you really want to make that difference, especially for those who are stuck in very difficult situations because of a complex series of problems that beget them, we really need to centre around the individual, not erode their aspiration to also want to play a part in solving their problems long term, but make sure that we scaffold them in the system.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will succeed but we will also fail, case-by-case.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will need to always recognise that when we make mistakes, we do not coordinate so well, do an after-action review and see how we can make it better and make the next case better managed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Member talked about the landscape in future being more SSO-centric.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I am wary to want to continue that mindset that the future is an SSO-centric one.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Because we started off with many helping hands and we want to have many helping hands working hand-in-hand and we have SSOs that work on the ground together with community partners and sense-making the issues on the ground.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Now, we are trying to have the SSOs play a little bit more of a coordinating role, providing information about needs on the ground and supporting individuals by marshalling themselves or through a lead agency identified for a particular case to assist.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In the social service sector and in the realm of volunteerism, none of us, no volunteer, no VWO would feel very encouraged if they were to be told to operate like automatons.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Everyone gives because they have the desire to want to contribute.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And so even as we try to provide more holistic support to individuals through case coordination, the key is to retain and to, in fact, strengthen the autonomy and desire of those, including VWOs, who wish to do good.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Enable them by partnering one another and with us, the SSOs, to better provide support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We want to strike a balance and make sure that we strengthen the social service sector and volunteering sector but, at the same time, secure better outcomes for those in need.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In terms of ensuring that our SSOs get the muscle, the resource and the influence to be able to achieve greater outcomes, this is something that we need to work with internally but also work through the network that I talked about on the ground.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But it involves building a network comprising many existing networks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If I know you and I am from one FSC and you are from another FSC, and we can find a way to work together to better help this family, it is that personal touch and the willingness to communicate that can sometimes make that difference to the family.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On the Member's point about the Enabling Masterplan, I share the Member's anxiety that having participated very actively in producing a very important roadmap to strengthen and enable Singaporeans with disability that the Member and others who are heavily involved in the process would like to know where we are.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There is no time or space during clarification to provide a full update, but I assure the Member and others that we would provide a proper update and we would involve the sector in the implementation and will continue to hear from you, listen to you and work alongside you.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On the three points the Member raised on the respite programme pilot terminating, whether, apart from the Mayflower programme, we will be able to work with people with hearing impairment to do pilots in preschool as well as sheltered enterprises in the community, these are all details that we will work very closely with the Member on and with the disability sector on.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: This clarification is for the Senior Parliamentary Secretary.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Given the digital trends, I had asked what the plans are in terms of the early childhood sector in helping young families and children prepare for the digital world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We agree with the Member that young children need to be prepared for the digital world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In fact, we realise and we also share that technology can play a very important role in the learning experience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: They found it a worthwhile opportunity for the kids to interact and be open and forthcoming in the process of learning, using a digital perspective.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Earlier, the Senior Parliamentary Secretary addressed the query I had regarding the solutions for the tight manpower situation for the preschool sector.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary had indicated that there were innovative strategies to deal with this.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Can I check how many preschools are using the technological solutions in the schools and how have these been improving their productivity?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We realise that, by doing this, it will bring lots of benefits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In some centres, if you look at it, they have enjoyed a savings of as much as 270 man-hours a month.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, it shows that the preschools and operators can benefit a lot by using smart solutions and we want to encourage more take-up rates.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Now that MSF is playing a much larger role in funding services and programmes, how does MSF also ensure that it does not erode the role of the community in giving them the space to continue to provide resources for the less fortunate?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think the Member hit the nail on the head.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Even as the Government does more, the community also should step up more.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That is what we see, both existing organisations and new ones coming forward to meet the needs of vulnerable Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We also see a lot of informal giving and informal volunteering within the community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: None of what we intend to do should nudge that out because that really strengthens us collectively as a society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Member is right that MSF funds a lot of services in the social service sector, especially key ones that we think are important to have alongside what we do in the Government, such as FSCs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Even then, there is always that element for the VWO which takes up that MSF-funded service to contribute to their own fundraising or develop their own complementary programmes that can operate out of those centres.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There is also a wide range of services and programmes run by VWOs in the rest of the social service centres.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, in NCSS, there are more than 460 social service VWOs and they serve a whole range of needs in society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: ComChest, for instance, supports more than 80 smaller VWOs and fundraise for them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There are matching schemes that help supplement what the VWOs raise to run their own schemes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The VWO sector came in in the early years when they saw needs and gaps.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And increasingly, as the Government does more in some of these areas, we build that partnership with them and work with them to tackle some of the challenges that they have been working on for many years.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Would the mover wish to withdraw the amendment?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Our appreciation also goes to all the other important stakeholders in this sector, from the hardworking and caring staff at the Ministry, to the social workers at VWOs, SSOs, FSCs and many others.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Your work and your empathy assure the heartbeat of our country remains warm, caring and inclusive for everyone.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: With that, Sir, I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.00 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.40 pm until 4.00 pm.
